title.text:
Language models and
building with them

objects.text: What does a language model do, how do we test one, and how do we make it answer from our own documents?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 22 of 24  |  Module E: Neural networks and text
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes: Welcome back. Last session we turned customer messages into numbers. Today we look at the technology behind chat assistants: language models. You will see what they actually do, why they sometimes invent things, and how to make one answer from your own documents. We build the search part ourselves in plain Python over the eight Lakeside Mart policies, and we test it with a list of twelve questions.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can explain tokens, the context window, prompts and hallucination in plain words. You can build retrieval over a small set of documents and score it with precision at k and recall at k, using an evaluation set you write yourself.

And you can use AI tools safely: you know what not to paste into a tool you do not control, and you know how to record AI-assisted work in an audit log. All of it runs on the eight Lakeside Mart policy documents.

title.text:
Your two hours: concepts first, then
a Python lab on policy documents

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x2.95_83d54561.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Pictures and plain words first. Then you open the notebook. Then the checks and what you keep.

slides.notes:
Two hours, in the same shape as before. Ten minutes of recall and the question of the day. Then forty-five minutes of concepts with laptops closed. After the break, forty-five minutes in a Colab notebook: you split the policies into chunks, build a retrieval function, write and score an evaluation set, and build a grounded prompt.

An optional last cell runs a small open model. The final ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep. Please protect the lab time.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Why must text become numbers before a model can compare two messages?
2.  What does TF-IDF do to a word that is found in almost every message?
3.  What is semantic search meant to find that a keyword search misses?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 21. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Why must text become numbers before a model can compare two messages?

A good answer is this. A model only does arithmetic. A bag of words, TF-IDF or an embedding gives each message a vector it can measure.

Question two. What does TF-IDF do to a word that is found in almost every message?

A good answer is this. It gives the word a weight near zero, so rare words count more.

Question three. What is semantic search meant to find that a keyword search misses?

A good answer is this. Messages with a similar meaning but different words, such as crowded cashier and a long queue.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 21

rows.text: Why must text become numbers before a model can compare two messages?
A model only does arithmetic. A bag of words, TF-IDF or an embedding gives each message a vector it can measure.
What does TF-IDF do to a word that is found in almost every message?
It gives the word a weight near zero, so rare words count more.
What is semantic search meant to find that a keyword search misses?
Messages with a similar meaning but different words, such as crowded cashier and a long queue.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.50.png

slides.notes:
Here are the answers to the three warm-up questions. A model only does arithmetic, so a message must become a vector first, by counting words, by TF-IDF or by an embedding. TF-IDF gives a word that appears in almost every message a weight near zero, so rare words count more.

And semantic search aims to find messages with a similar meaning but different words. I say aims, because you check that claim yourself with a precision score. Which answer needs more practice?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A token is a word or piece of a word that a language model reads and writes. The context window is how many tokens it can read at once.
The instruction you give a model. A system prompt sets rules. Zero-shot gives no examples. Few-shot gives a few worked examples.
Fluent text that no source supports. It can read well and still be false.
Find the relevant chunks of your documents first (retrieval and ranking), then ask the model to answer from them (grounding).
Evaluation set (precision at k, recall at k)
A labelled list of test questions with the right passage. Precision at k and recall at k score the search.

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_0.34.png

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Token and context window. A token is a word or piece of a word that a language model reads and writes. The context window is how many tokens it can read at once.

Prompt (system prompt, zero-shot, few-shot). The instruction you give a model. A system prompt sets rules. Zero-shot gives no examples. Few-shot gives a few worked examples.

Hallucination. Fluent text that no source supports. It can read well and still be false.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Find the relevant chunks of your documents first (retrieval and ranking), then ask the model to answer from them (grounding).

Evaluation set (precision at k, recall at k). A labelled list of test questions with the right passage. Precision at k and recall at k score the search.

title.text:
A language model reads and writes tokens:
words, pieces of words and punctuation

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_tokens_11.90x4.25_9f709beb.png
objects.alt: A language model reads and writes tokens: words, pieces of words and punctuation

objects.text: Illustrative split and made-up numbers. A real tokeniser cuts and numbers text in its own way.

slides.notes:
A language model does not read letters or whole sentences. It reads tokens. A token is a word, a piece of a word or a punctuation mark, and each token has a number in the model's list. Tokenisation is the step that cuts text into tokens. In this picture, Lakeside is cut into Lake and side, and the full stop is its own token.

The split and the numbers are made up to show the idea, because every model has its own list. Notice that six words became eight tokens. Models, prices and limits are counted in tokens. Why might a long word cost more tokens?

title.text:
Next-token prediction: the model scores
every possible next token and picks one

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_nextword_7.70x4.80_df476db8.png
objects.alt: Next-token prediction: the model scores every possible next token and picks one

objects.text: A language model is trained to predict the next token from the tokens before it.

runs.text: The bars come from counting our own 800 messages.
A large model does the same job with a neural network that reads the whole context.
It scores every token it knows, then picks one.

slides.notes:
The core job of a language model is next-token prediction. To show the idea, I built a tiny model from our eight hundred feedback messages. It only counts which word follows was. After was, the word not came 19 times out of 179, charged 17 times, and so on.

That is 21 different words, with no clear winner. A large language model does the same job, but it uses a neural network that reads the whole context. Published research describes such models as trained to predict the next token. Why would one word of context make a poor predictor?

title.text:
One answer is built one token at a
time: read, score, pick, add, repeat

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_b4e8bce7.png
objects.alt: One answer is built one token at a time: read, score, pick, add, repeat

objects.text: A 40-token answer means 40 trips round this loop.

slides.notes:
Here is the loop behind every answer from a chat assistant. The model reads the text so far, which is your prompt and anything it has already written. It scores every possible next token. It picks one. The picked token is added to the text, and the loop starts again with one more token to read.

It stops when it picks a token that means stop. So a long answer is many small guesses in a row, each one made from everything written so far. Nothing in the loop looks a fact up. Which step do you think makes the same question give two different answers?

title.text:
The context window limits how many tokens a model
can read at once, so we send only what matters

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_context_11.90x4.25_a00061e0.png
objects.alt: The context window limits how many tokens a model can read at once, so we send only what matters

objects.text: Prompt, pasted text and answer share one window. Word counts: our grounded prompt.

slides.notes:
The context window is how many tokens a model can read at once. Everything counts against it: your prompt, any text you paste, and the answer so far. Window sizes differ between models and keep changing, so check the documentation of the one you use. The top bar is a whole document library, which is hypothetical here, and it would not fit in any window.

The bottom bar is what retrieval sends for one question in our lab: a short rule, three chunks and the question, 95 words in total. That is the idea behind retrieval. Why would sending less text sometimes give a better answer?

title.text:
A prompt is your instruction: a system prompt sets
rules, and examples turn zero-shot into few-shot

rows.text: Rules and role, set once for the whole conversation
Answer only from the passages. If the answer is missing, say so.
A task with no worked examples
Label this message as positive, neutral or negative: Slow service at the counter.
A task with a few worked examples first
Fast checkout. Label: positive. Charged twice. Label: negative. Is milk available? Label:

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_shield_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_doc_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_notebook_0.50.png

slides.notes:
A prompt is the instruction you give a model. A system prompt sets rules and a role once, for example answer only from the passages. A zero-shot prompt gives the task with no examples. A few-shot prompt puts a few worked examples first, so the model sees the pattern before the real case.

These are different ways of writing the input. They change what the model is likely to write, but they do not make it check a fact. The examples on the slide are from our feedback data. Which kind would you try first for labelling messages?

title.text:
Temperature is a setting that makes the
next-token pick more repeatable or more varied

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_temperature_7.70x4.80_32f5b8fc.png
objects.alt: Temperature is a setting that makes the next-token pick more repeatable or more varied

objects.text: Many tools offer a setting called temperature. Check the tool documentation for what it does there.

runs.text: Low temperature: the top token wins more often.
High temperature: the choice spreads out.
Illustrative made-up scores for The queue was ...

slides.notes:
Temperature is a setting that many tools expose, and I only want you to know the name and the idea. Check the documentation of your own tool, because the details differ. In general, a low temperature makes the model pick the most likely token more often, so answers are more repeatable.

A high temperature spreads the choice, so answers vary more. The picture uses made-up scores for four words after The queue was. At temperature one half the top word gets about eighty percent. At two it gets about forty two percent. For a policy answer, which would you want?

title.text:
Hallucination: a model can write a
fluent answer that no source supports

objects.text: No policy given

runs.text: Question: How long do points last?
A model can still write a smooth answer with a guessed number of months (hypothetical).
Nothing can be checked.

objects.text: Policy passage given

runs.text: Passage: Points expire after 12 months.
The answer can quote the passage.
You can check it against the source.

objects.text: Give the model the source. Check the answer.

slides.notes:
Hallucination means fluent text that no source supports. The model writes likely text, so if the policy is not in its prompt, it can still write a smooth answer, perhaps with a guessed number of months. The left example is hypothetical: I did not run a model. On the right, the passage Points expire after twelve months is in the prompt.

Now the answer can quote it, and you can check it against the source. That is the whole idea of retrieval-augmented generation. Hallucination does not disappear, but it becomes checkable. Which of your own documents would you want an assistant to answer from?

title.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) finds the
relevant chunks first, then answers from them

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_ef2cb844.png
objects.alt: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) finds the relevant chunks first, then answers from them

objects.text: We build the first three steps in numpy today, and score them with an evaluation set.

slides.notes:
This is the whole RAG pattern. First, chunking: split the documents into short pieces. Second, retrieval: find the chunks closest to the question. Third, ranking: sort them by similarity and keep the top k. Fourth, grounding: put those chunks in the prompt and tell the model to answer only from them.

Fifth, the model answers and you check the answer against the source chunk. Today we build the first three steps ourselves, in plain numpy, and we measure how well they work. Why do we need to measure retrieval separately from the answer?

title.text:
Chunking splits each document into short
pieces: the 8 policies become 59 chunks

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_chunks_11.90x4.25_a24c09e3.png
objects.alt: Chunking splits each document into short pieces: the 8 policies become 59 chunks

objects.text: Here one sentence is one chunk. Small chunks are precise. Large ones keep context.

slides.notes:
Chunking means splitting a document into pieces that can be found and sent separately. Here the loyalty policy has 9 chunks, one per sentence. Across all 8 policy files we get 59 chunks of about 12 words each. Chunk size is a design choice. Small chunks are precise but can lose context.

Large chunks keep context but bring in unrelated text and use more of the context window. Each chunk keeps its file name, so we can say where an answer came from. Would you ever split a contract differently from a menu?

title.text:
Retrieval scores every chunk against the
question, and ranking keeps the top k

rows.text: Customers may return an item within 7 days of purchase with the till receipt. (returns_policy.txt)
A customer who finds an expired item should return it with the receipt for a full refund and the branch records the incident. (food_safety.txt)
Complaints from customers about a supplier's product are logged by item and branch and reviewed monthly by the buyer. (supplier_complaints.txt)

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png

objects.text: Question: "How many days do I have to return an item?" TF-IDF cosine similarity over 59 chunks and a vocabulary of 293 different words, as in Session 21.

slides.notes:
Here is retrieval on one question: how many days do I have to return an item?

We use the same TF-IDF and cosine similarity as last session, now over the 59 chunks. Every chunk gets a score, and ranking sorts them. The top chunk, from the returns policy, scores 0.56 and contains the answer: within seven days. The second and third chunks only share words such as return and customer, so they are wrong.

This is keyword retrieval, because it matches words. Retrieval based on embeddings works the same way with different vectors. How would you know the second chunk is wrong without reading it?

title.text:
Grounding: put the retrieved chunk in the
prompt and tell the model to answer only from it

objects.text: A grounded prompt with k = 1. The lab builds the same prompt with k = 3.
System prompt
Answer only from the passages below. If the answer is not in the passages, say: I could not find that in the policies.
Passage
Customers may return an item within 7 days of purchase with the till receipt.
Question
How many days do I have to return an item?

slides.notes:
Grounding means tying the answer to retrieved text. The prompt has three parts. The system prompt tells the model to answer only from the passages, and to say so if the answer is missing. The passage is the top chunk from retrieval, which is the returns policy sentence.

And the question is the learner question. In the lab you build this prompt for the top three chunks, which is 95 words. The instruction to say I could not find that is important, because it gives the model a safe way out. A model might still ignore an instruction, so you still check the answer.

What could go wrong if the retrieved chunk is wrong?

title.text:
An evaluation set is a labelled list of test
questions with the right passage for each

rows.text: How many days do I have to return an item?
How long do mobile money refunds take?
Which towns does delivery not reach?
What is the delivery fee within 5 kilometres?
What percent discount do Gold customers get?
How long is customer data kept?
What temperature must dairy be stored at?
When do branches open on Sunday?
What happens when more than 5 percent of a delivery is damaged?
Does Lakeside Mart ask for my PIN?
Can points be exchanged for cash?

slides.notes:
To know whether retrieval works, you need an evaluation set: a labelled test set of questions where you know the right passage in advance. Here are twelve questions, with the policy file that holds the answer. For each one, I copied the answer sentence word for word from the file, and the code confirms that exactly one chunk contains it.

That chunk is the relevant chunk. Twelve is a small set, so treat the scores as a first look: one question moves a score by 0.08, so write thirty or more before you choose between methods. You write more in the lab. A good evaluation set includes easy and hard questions.

Which of these would you expect to be hard for a keyword search?

title.text:
Precision at k and recall at k
score the top k results of a search

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_rank_7.70x4.80_7429310b.png
objects.alt: Precision at k and recall at k score the top k results of a search

objects.text: Precision at k: how many of the top k results are right. Recall at k: how many of all the right chunks were found.

runs.text: Illustrative: 3 chunks are right in total.
Top 5 hold 2 of them: precision at 5 = 2/5 = 0.4.
Recall at 5 = 2/3 = 0.67.

slides.notes:
Here is a made-up ranked list. The search returned five chunks, and the gold ones are the relevant chunks. Three chunks in the library are right in total, and the top five hold two of them. Precision at k is the share of the k results that are right: two out of five, which is 0.4.

Recall at k is the share of all the right chunks that were found: two out of three, which is 0.67. Precision tells you how clean the results are. Recall tells you how much you missed. Which one matters more when a wrong chunk can lead to a wrong answer?

title.text:
Precision at k and recall at k are
two ratios of the same count

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.96_34ba8d07.png
objects.alt: Precision at k and recall at k are two ratios of the same count

rows.text: How many top results we look at
Results in the top k that contain the answer
right chunk at rank 4: P@3 = 0, R@3 = 0

slides.notes:
Here are the two formulas. Precision at k divides the number of relevant chunks in the top k by k. Recall at k divides it by the number of all relevant chunks. Worked example one: for the return question, the right chunk is at rank one, so among the top three there is one right chunk.

Precision at three is one third, 0.33, and recall at three is one out of one, 1.00. Worked example two: for how long do points last, the right chunk is only at rank 4, so the top three hold none, and both scores are zero. With one right chunk per question, recall at k is the same as asking whether it is in the top k.

Why is precision at three limited to one third here?

title.text:
On our twelve questions, keyword
retrieval puts the right chunk first 10 times

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_prk_7.70x4.80_779d935a.png
objects.alt: On our twelve questions, keyword retrieval puts the right chunk first 10 times

objects.text: Precision at 1 is 0.83. Recall at 5 is 1.00.

runs.text: Mean over 12 questions, TF-IDF cosine retrieval.
Precision falls as k grows, because only one chunk is right.
Recall rises as k grows.

slides.notes:
These are the real scores of our TF-IDF retrieval over the twelve questions. At k equal one, precision and recall are both 0.83: the right chunk was first for 10 of twelve questions. At k equal three, precision is 0.31 and recall is 0.92. At five, recall reaches 1.00, so the right chunk is always in the top five.

Precision falls as k grows because only one chunk per question is right. So the choice of k is a trade-off: a larger k finds more but sends more text to the model. Which k would you choose for a customer assistant?

title.text:
Read the failures: two questions
whose right chunk is not first, and why

rows.text: Data is kept for 3 years after the last purchase. (data_privacy.txt)
The word last matches last purchase. The right chunk, Points expire after 12 months, says expire. It is at rank 4.
Which towns does delivery not reach?
The title chunk repeats the word delivery. The right chunk is at rank 2.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png

objects.text: Fixes to try: drop title chunks, add synonyms, or use embeddings. Then score again on the same set.

slides.notes:
Always read the failures. For how long do points last, the top result is about data privacy, because the word last also appears in last purchase. The policy says expire, a different word for the same idea, so a keyword search cannot connect them. The right chunk is at rank 4.

For which towns does delivery not reach, the top result is the title chunk, Lakeside Mart Delivery, which repeats the word delivery. The right chunk is at rank 2. Both fixes are cheap to try: drop the title chunks, or use embeddings, which are built for different words with the same meaning.

Then you score again on the same set. Why must you keep the set fixed while you test a fix?

title.text:
A small open model can run inside your own
Colab notebook to write the grounded answer

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_f6993616.png
objects.alt: A small open model can run inside your own Colab notebook to write the grounded answer

objects.text: Optional lab step. Small models can be wrong or ignore rules, so checking is not optional.

slides.notes:
This is the last piece of RAG: generation. You can run a small open model inside your own Colab notebook, with no account and no paid service. We use SmolLM2 360M Instruct, a small open model whose model card lists the Apache 2.0 licence, and you should read the model card for any model you use at work.

Colab limits change, so check the current ones. You download the model once, build the grounded prompt from the top chunks, and generate a short answer. No model output appears in this deck, because it was not run when the deck was written. Small models can be wrong or ignore your rules, so the last step is always to check against the source chunk.

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: The splitter also cut after abbreviations or headings.
Split only after a full stop that is followed by a capital letter.
The policy folder is not next to the notebook.
Run the first cell again and check that data.zip was unpacked.
You divided by the number of relevant chunks.
Precision divides by k. Recall divides by all relevant.
The question has no word in the vocabulary.
Check the stop words and the lowercase step.
A small model can ignore instructions.
Write it in your audit log, and trust the source chunk instead.

Five messages you may meet. More chunks than fifty nine means the splitter also cut after abbreviations, so split only after a full stop and a capital letter. A file not found error means the policy folder is not next to the notebook, so run the first cell again.

A precision of one at k equals three means you divided by the number of relevant chunks. Precision divides by k. Scores that are all zero mean the question had no word in the vocabulary. And a small model that ignores the passage is a finding, so record it in your audit log. Read the message first. It usually tells you the answer.

Hallucination. Retrieve the passage, ground the prompt in it, and check the answer against the source.
